Snippet: Numerous preclinical data and Phase I/II clinical trials have demonstrated the effectiveness of hyperthermia as a radiation sensitizer and inhibitor of radiation damage repair. Similar effects of heat have been reported for tumors exposed to radiation (Sneed et al., 2004;Seegenschmiedt et al., 1995Seegenschmiedt et al., , 1996 which has motivated the development of hyperthermia devices capable of delivering localized heat to tumor targets in order to spare adjacent normal tissues and critical organs (Stauffer, 2005). Localized hyperthermia at moderate temperatures (40-45 °C) delivered as an adjuvant for radiation and chemotherapy has been reported to improve local control and survival rate for various tumors (Jones et al., 2005;Jones et al., 2003;Perez et al., 1991;Sherar et al., 1997;Sneed et al., 2004;Sneed et al., 1998;van der Zee et al., 2000;Vernon, 1994;Vernon et al., 1996). Furthermore, preclinical work has shown that reducing the time interval between radiation and heat treatments increases the TER of thermoradiotherapy from 1.5 for sequential treatments to 2.5 or higher when heat and radiation are applied simultaneously (Overgaard, 1980). Early clinical results that used linear accelerator and cobalt-60 radiation with commercial hyperthermia applicator demonstrated the feasibility of concurrent thermoradiotherapy (Moros et al., 1995b;Myerson et al., 1999). Encouraging preliminary results led to the development of combination applicators such as the scanning ultrasound reflector linear array system (SURLAS) (Moros et al., 1995a;Novak et al., 2005;Novak et al., 2008) and the conformal thermobrachytherapy applicator of this study (Juang et al., 2006;Stauffer et al., 2004;Stauffer et al., 2005;Taschereau et al., 2004). Title: Nanoparticles in enhancing microwave imaging and microwave Hyperthermia effect for liver cancer treatment
Snippet: In 2019, an expected 42,030 adults (29,480 men and 12,550 women) in the United States will be diagnosed with primary liver cancer. Since 1980, the percentage of liver cancer has tripled. Between 2006 and 2015, the number of cases diagnosed with the disease increased by around 3% annually. Men are about 3 times more likely than women to be diagnosed with the liver cancer [1]. Severe patients that cannot undergo surgical resection are eligible for hyperthermia which is a new therapeutic method that consists in heating the tumor cells in order to make selective damage. Final temperatures can range between 42 ∘ C to 45 ∘ C (mild hyperthermia) [2]. 

Currently, two frequencies -915 and 2.4 GHz -are utilized in microwave hyperthermia; the frequency of 2.4 GHz is commonly applied in the clinic. Compared with 2.4 GHz microwaves, 915 MHz microwaves have a larger penetration depth. Besides, the energy attenuation of 915 MHz microwaves is less than that of 2.4 GHz microwaves and more electromagnetic energy may convert into heat energy. Therefore, 915 MHz microwaves can provide a larger hyperthermia zone [3,4]. 

Nevertheless, achieving localized hyperthermia of the cancer cells without harming the nearby healthy tissue still challenges [5]. This study proposes to utilize nanoparticles as microwave absorbers to realize localized heating under microwave radiation which has been investigated for prevention, treatment, and early diagnosis of cancer, since nanoparticles can accumulate around or inside malignant regions, to aid localized heating only affecting tumors. Approaches to nanoparticle-mediated hyperthermia include plasmonic photothermal therapy (PPTT), magnetically induced heating [6], and microwave irradiation. For PPTT methods, gold nanoparticles can possess greatly enhanced visible and near-infrared light absorption due to the phenomenon of surface Plasmon resonance. Unfortunately, the penetration depth of near-infrared light in the human body is only a few millimeters due to notable scattering and attenuation of light by biological tissues. Furthermore, the toxicity of a surfactant utilized in gold nanoparticle synthesis can degrade membranes and peptides.

Title: Documentation of a New Intracavitary Applicator for Transrectal Hyperthermia Designed for Prostate Cancer Cases: A Phantom Study
Snippet: Concerning clinical trials, intracavitary hyperthermia has already shown antitumor activity and has a potential role in the treatment of prostate cancer. The aim of this study was to document a new intracavitary applicator operating at 433 MHz, designed for transrectal hyperthermia, as well as to assess the specific absorption rate (SAR) distributions in terms of temperature measurements in a soft-tissue phantom. The microwave applicator consists of a dipole-type λ/2, a reflector, and the cooling system. The applicator was placed into a soft-tissue gel-phantom box that was mimicking the dielectric properties of the normal tissue. A calibrated thermometer was implanted inside the phantom at specific locations, to calculate temperature distributions. snippet.text:
In 2019, an expected 42,030 adults (29,480 men and 12,550 women) in the United States will be diagnosed with primary liver cancer. Since 1980, the percentage of liver cancer has tripled. Between 2006 and 2015, the number of cases diagnosed with the disease increased by around 3% annually. Men are about 3 times more likely than women to be diagnosed with the liver cancer [1]. Severe patients that cannot undergo surgical resection are eligible for hyperthermia which is a new therapeutic method that consists in heating the tumor cells in order to make selective damage. Final temperatures can range between 42 ∘ C to 45 ∘ C (mild hyperthermia) [2]. 

Currently, two frequencies -915 and 2.4 GHz -are utilized in microwave hyperthermia; the frequency of 2.4 GHz is commonly applied in the clinic. Compared with 2.4 GHz microwaves, 915 MHz microwaves have a larger penetration depth. Besides, the energy attenuation of 915 MHz microwaves is less than that of 2.4 GHz microwaves and more electromagnetic energy may convert into heat energy. Therefore, 915 MHz microwaves can provide a larger hyperthermia zone [3,4]. 

Nevertheless, achieving localized hyperthermia of the cancer cells without harming the nearby healthy tissue still challenges [5]. This study proposes to utilize nanoparticles as microwave absorbers to realize localized heating under microwave radiation which has been investigated for prevention, treatment, and early diagnosis of cancer, since nanoparticles can accumulate around or inside malignant regions, to aid localized heating only affecting tumors. Approaches to nanoparticle-mediated hyperthermia include plasmonic photothermal therapy (PPTT), magnetically induced heating [6], and microwave irradiation. For PPTT methods, gold nanoparticles can possess greatly enhanced visible and near-infrared light absorption due to the phenomenon of surface Plasmon resonance. Unfortunately, the penetration depth of near-infrared light in the human body is only a few millimeters due to notable scattering and attenuation of light by biological tissues. Furthermore, the toxicity of a surfactant utilized in gold nanoparticle synthesis can degrade membranes and peptides.

The SAR experimental measurements showed that our applicator might be used effectively as a treatment device for prostate cancer, demonstrating a clear advantage over other similar transrectal devices.

Introduction and clinical context of deep microwave hyperthermia in prostate cancer
Deep microwave hyperthermia (DH) delivers localized, high-temperature heat (typically 40–47°C, often quantified as CEM43 in the 25–200 min range) to the prostate using microwave antennas or capacitive couplers, aiming to raise tumor temperatures while sparing normal tissue as much as possible. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heating of tumor cells in the 40–47 °C range with cumulative equivalent minutes at 43 °C (CEM43) of 25–200 min has been associated with radiosensitizing effects</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Microwave and radiofrequency hyperthermia generate heat via electromagnetic fields that drive water molecule rotation and frictional heating</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Radiofrequency capacitive hyperthermia is specifically recommended for prostate cancer due to cancer-versus-normal tissue autofocusing, where cancer’s physical properties cause preferential heating</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-2">In prostate modeling at 2.45 GHz, perfusion strongly modulates temperature distributions and necrosis, underscoring the need for accurate bioheat modeling to achieve deep tissue targets</cite>.

Core radiobiological mechanisms of thermoradiation synergy
1) DNA damage amplification and repair inhibition
<cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heat enhances radiosensitization by increasing DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and inhibiting DNA repair mechanisms, thereby intensifying radiation-induced toxicity</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">At 42–45 °C, hyperthermia is described as a potent radiosensitizer that can cause irreversible damage due to protein degradation and the lack of DSB repair in cells</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">In early combined modality experiments, 43 °C for 1 hour with single doses of 5–10 Gy produced higher cytotoxicity than radiation alone, and 10 Gy combined with 44 °C microwave heat significantly enhanced cell death in breast cancer models</cite>. Mechanistically, heat can directly damage DNA and also increase the formation of DSBs during or after irradiation, while concurrently suppressing key repair pathways such as non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR), thereby increasing the likelihood of lethal chromosomal aberrations. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Application of hyperthermia was reported to increase tumor radiosensitivity by enhancing DNA damage and inhibition of DNA repair mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">The additive effect of hyperthermia plus radiation can be quantified by the thermal enhancement factor (TEF), defined as the ratio of the response after radiation with heat to the response after radiation alone at the same dose</cite>.

2) Oxygenation and hypoxia modulation
<cite id="28e53f6b-0">Hyperthermia reduces hypoxia, thereby sensitizing radiation-resistant hypoxic tumor cells</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">The addition of heat to radiation inhibits DSB repair and intensifies radiation toxicity, with the radiosensitizing effect linked to improved oxygenation in hypoxic fractions</cite>. In prostate cancer, where hypoxia is common and linked to poor outcomes, microwave HT can preferentially raise tumor pO2 by heating and vascular effects, improving the effectiveness of fractionated RT that relies on oxygen-dependent repair pathways. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">High-energy photon RT (6–18 MV) is used for deeper prostate penetration, and combining heat with radiation is motivated by the need to overcome hypoxia in deep-seated tumors</cite>.

3) Cell-cycle, apoptosis, and heat shock protein (HSP) signaling
<cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heating can trigger apoptosis through inhibition of heat shock proteins and direct DNA damage</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Hyperthermia-induced upregulation of Hsp72 increases radio- and chemo-sensitivity of prostate cancer cells by suppressing survival, MAPK, and NF-κB pathways, and this radiosensitization has been validated in an in vivo mouse prostate cancer model</cite>. HSPs act as signaling and transcriptional mediators under heat stress; their induction can suppress pro-survival signaling that otherwise counteracts radiation-induced damage, thereby allowing more efficient execution of apoptotic programs following irradiation. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Concurrently, heat can increase extracellular HSPs during tumor necrosis, which induces immunity against tumor cells, but some studies report roles for Hsp70 and Hsp72 in radioresistance or apoptosis resistance, indicating that the net effect depends on expression levels and isoform-specific functions</cite>.

Non-thermal microwave electrophysiology and oxidative stress mechanisms
Beyond thermal dosimetry, microwave fields can induce non-thermal biological effects that potentiate radiation responses. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Microwave and radiofrequency heating rely on electromagnetic interactions with tissue water; precise dosimetry is challenging and reproducibility can be limited, but mechanistically heat production drives downstream cellular effects</cite>. <cite id="eb2fc70f-0">Prostate cancer cells exhibit elevated baseline oxidative stress and express ROS sources such as NOX enzymes and mitochondrial metabolism; tumor antioxidant capacity is often impaired, with increased lipid, protein, and nucleic acid oxidation correlating with aggressiveness</cite>. <cite id="eb2fc70f-1">Oxidative stress promotes DNA adducts, lipid peroxidation, protein carbonylation, mitochondrial abnormalities, and aberrant apoptosis, linking ROS accumulation to prostate carcinogenesis</cite>. Microwave-induced heating can further elevate mitochondrial ROS and perturb membrane/calcium homeostasis, augmenting radiation-induced oxidative DNA damage and impairing DNA repair enzymes and replication machinery during or after irradiation. <cite id="eb2fc70f-2">ROS and oxidative stress are excessively produced when cells are subjected to physical environments, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, and androgen receptor signaling dynamically regulates NRF2-mediated oxidative stress responses in PCa</cite>. <cite id="eb2fc70f-3">Systematic reviews in prostate cancer report significantly higher oxidative stress markers and impaired antioxidant defenses compared to controls, supporting a role for ROS-centric mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Microwave/radiofrequency hyperthermia has been shown to enhance radiosensitization via inhibition of DNA repair mechanisms and induction of apoptosis, consistent with oxidative and electrophysiologic perturbations that increase radiosensitivity</cite>.

Immune modulation: danger signals, antigen release, and dendritic-cell activation
Heat and thermal injury trigger immunogenic responses that can synergize with radiation. <cite id="bd38702b-1">Heat shock proteins act as chaperones that stimulate dendritic cell maturation and present tumor antigens, priming antigen-specific T cells; local tumor necrosis releases danger signals and neoantigens that are taken up by professional antigen-presenting cells, culminating in antitumor adaptive immunity</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Prostate cancer models demonstrate that hyperthermia-induced Hsp72 increases sensitivity to radio- and chemotherapy via suppression of survival signaling, and extracellular HSPs released during necrosis promote immunity against tumor cells</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-3">Thermal ablation in cancers including prostate increases PSA and induces upregulation of danger signals such as HSP70, with increased dendritic cell numbers and maturation, supporting enhanced antigen cross-presentation and T-cell priming</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-2">Heating increases extracellular HSP release and activates innate immune effector cells (NK cells via NKG2D, macrophages, and dendritic cells), enabling DC uptake of HSP/tumor antigen complexes, migration to lymph nodes, T-cell activation, and delivery of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells to tumors</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-4">Mild hyperthermia enhances anti-tumor immune responses by promoting HSP-mediated antigen cross-presentation and augmenting MHC class I antigen presentation, thereby improving CTL responses</cite>. Importantly, radiation can further amplify these immune effects, potentially enhancing immunogenic cell death and immune memory, while heat improves the quality and quantity of tumor antigens and danger cues presented to the immune system.

Tumor microenvironment: perfusion, necrosis/edema, and radiosensitization interplay
The depth and heterogeneity of prostate tumors impose constraints on heating and repair dynamics. <cite id="28e53f6b-2">Microwave (2.45 GHz) fields applied as internal sources show that blood perfusion critically shapes temperature distributions and the evolution of thermal damage, with higher perfusion increasing heat loss and altering necrotic percentages</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Early combined heat and radiation experiments showed enhanced cytotoxicity at clinically relevant temperatures (43 °C for 1 h) even when delivered during or around irradiation, suggesting that perfusion-mediated heat dissipation can be managed to achieve synergistic effects</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-2">Hyperthermia increases perfusion and oxygenation of hypoxic tumor cells, and acts in acidic pH and the radioresistant S-phase, complementing radiation whose free-radical DNA damage is potentiated by heat-inhibited repair</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heating can also reduce hypoxia and induce apoptosis via HSP inhibition, thereby increasing the fraction of cells irreversibly damaged by ionizing radiation</cite>. Clinically, heat-driven edema and transient perfusion changes must be managed around RT to avoid dose interruptions; modeling-guided planning and temperature monitoring can mitigate these effects and preserve synergy.

Scheduling, dose, and prostate-specific translational evidence
Prostate trials of capacitive RF/microwave HT typically deliver heat pre- or post-RT to enhance DSB effects or sensitize sublethal repair. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Prostate RF capacitive HT at 13.56 MHz induces preferential tissue heating via dielectric coupling, and combined modality studies show that heat before or after irradiation can enhance radiation damage; the TEF quantifies this synergy, with studies in prostate cancer cells exploring pre- and post-treatment schedules</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">In combined water-bath hyperthermia with RT, cytotoxicity peaked after 43 °C for 1 hour followed by 5–10 Gy, and microwave heat at 44 °C for 1 hour with 10 Gy significantly increased cell death hours later, supporting a time-dependent radiosensitization mechanism</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">High-dose photon RT is commonly used in prostate cancer; pairing heat with radiation leverages heat’s inhibition of DSB repair and its capacity to increase protein degradation, aligning with clinical efforts to escalate doses while controlling toxicity</cite>.

Mechanistic biomarkers and clinical predictors
Several candidate biomarkers may predict responsiveness to thermoradiation in prostate cancer. <cite id="eb2fc70f-0">NRF2 and related antioxidant pathways regulate ROS and metabolic shifts in PCa; oxidative stress levels and antioxidant capacity vary with disease aggressiveness, suggesting that tumors with higher basal ROS and impaired antioxidant defenses may be more radiosensitizable to heat</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">HSP72 induction and suppression of survival/MAPK/NF-κB pathways enhance radio-sensitivity in prostate models, whereas HSP70 or HSP72-mediated resistance has been reported in some contexts, implying isoform- and expression-dependent effects</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heating-induced inhibition of heat shock proteins and direct DNA damage promotes apoptosis, but the precise balance depends on the tumor’s thermoresistance and repair capacity</cite>. Clinically, reproducibility and dosimetry constraints remain: <cite id="28e53f6b-0">electromagnetic-wave HT methods can lack precision in target definition and allow only limited quantification of thermal dose without MR temperature mapping, highlighting the need for robust thermometry and quality assurance</cite>.

Putting it together: how deep microwave hyperthermia sensitizes prostate tumors to radiation
- Heat increases DSB formation and directly damages DNA, while suppressing non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination, leading to higher rates of misrepair or no-repair after irradiation. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Enhancing DNA damage and inhibiting DNA repair mechanisms under hyperthermia intensifies radiation-induced toxicity</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">At 42–45 °C, inhibition of DSB repair amplifies radiation damage</cite>.
- Microwave HT preferentially elevates tumor oxygenation and targets hypoxic subvolumes, improving oxygen-dependent repair inhibition and the efficacy of photon RT in deep-seated prostate tissue. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heat reduces hypoxia and increases radiosensitivity</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Radiation-induced DSBs are potentiated by heat that inhibits repair, with hypoxia as a key mediator</cite>.
- Electrophysiologic and oxidative effects from microwave heating (membrane/calcium perturbations, mitochondrial ROS) degrade DNA repair capacity and promote apoptosis, especially when aligned with irradiation timing. <cite id="eb2fc70f-0">ROS sources and impaired antioxidant defenses are intrinsic to aggressive PCa</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Microwave/radiofrequency heating enhances radiosensitization via repair inhibition and apoptosis induction</cite>.
- Heat-induced HSPs and DAMPs create a pro-immune microenvironment: extracellular HSPs, neoantigen release, and dendritic-cell maturation enhance CTL responses, which can amplify radiation-induced immunogenic cell death and drive systemic antitumor immunity. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Hsp72-mediated suppression of survival signaling increases radiosensitivity in prostate models and extracellular HSPs promote immunity</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-1">HSPs chaperone antigens to DCs and drive T-cell priming</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-3">Prostate ablation increases PSA and induces HSP70 upregulation with increased dendritic cell maturation</cite>.
- Delivery physics and tumor physics shape synergy: deep microwave applicators (endorectal/corporal or interstitial antennas) must overcome perfusion cooling to reach 40–43 °C targets in the prostate, and TEF-based scheduling (pre- vs post-RT) can be optimized to maximize DSB fixation and minimize repair. <cite id="28e53f6b-2">Perfusion strongly modulates deep-tissue heating and necrosis</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">TEF quantifies the additive effect of heat and radiation, with prostate-specific scheduling studies guiding pre/post-irradiation strategies</cite>.

Clinical integration and open questions
<cite id="28e53f6b-0">Early combined hyperthermia–radiation studies in prostate and other models demonstrate significant enhancement of cytotoxicity at clinically achievable temperatures (43–44 °C for 1 h) and doses (5–10 to 10 Gy)</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Capacitive RF HT is recommended for prostate cancer due to autofocusing and preferential tumor heating, and the TEF framework is used to estimate and schedule synergistic gains</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">However, technical challenges remain in targeting precision and thermal dosimetry for electromagnetic-wave HT, with better thermometry (e.g., MR temperature mapping) enabling more reproducible, quantifiable dose delivery</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">HSP-mediated effects can be both beneficial and maladaptive depending on isoform and expression levels, indicating a need for biomarker-driven patient selection</cite>. <cite id="eb2fc70f-0">Given the central role of oxidative stress in PCa progression and treatment resistance, combining microwave HT with strategies that further elevate ROS while normalizing antioxidant capacity may maximize radiosensitization</cite>.

Summary
Deep microwave hyperthermia sensitizes prostate tumors to radiation through a coordinated set of thermal and non-thermal mechanisms: heat amplifies radiation-induced DNA damage while inhibiting repair, improves oxygenation in hypoxic prostate regions, triggers apoptosis via HSP modulation, and induces non-thermal electrophysiologic and oxidative perturbations that degrade repair capacity. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">These effects occur at clinically relevant temperatures (40–47 °C; CEM43 25–200 min) and have been demonstrated to increase cytotoxicity over RT alone in vitro and in vivo</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Prostate-focused RF/microwave HT leverages these pathways, with TEF-based scheduling and perfusion-aware delivery to enhance radiosensitization</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Immune mechanisms mediated by HSPs and DAMPs further potentiate antitumor immunity, creating a dual cytotoxic and immunologic synergy with radiation</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-2">Ultimately, modeling and clinical engineering must align deep tissue perfusion with thermal dose to ensure that these mechanistic advantages translate into reproducible, safe, and effective gains in prostate radiotherapy outcomes</cite>.

Title: NRF2: A crucial regulator for mitochondrial metabolic shift and prostate cancer progression

Title: Exploring experimental models of prostate cancer in chemoprevention: Oxidative stress as a key pathway to translational research
Snippet: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most common cancer in men globally, as well as a leading cause of cancer-related death. 1 PCa is positive for androgen receptor (AR) expression, and it exhibits androgendependent growth. 2 Thus, this malignancy significantly responds to androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT). However, castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), which has acquired castration-resistant growth, is metastatic and carries a poor prognosis. The process by which normal prostate cells become malignant involves a combination of various factors, including congenital factors determined by race, region, and genetics, 3,4 environmental factors such as dietary and other lifestyle habits; and acquired factors such as genetic changes. 

In particular, aging and diet and lifestyle habits can lead to changes in the endocrine environment of the prostate gland and chronic inflammation, which are associated with PCa development. An important mechanism of PCa development and progression is 'oxidative stress,' which arises from a redox imbalance between the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and activity of antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase (GPX, Figure 1). 5 Excessive ROS accumulation promotes the development of DNA adducts, lipid peroxidation, and protein carbonylation through the oxidation of nucleic acids and lipids, resulting in mitochondrial abnormalities, abnormal apoptosis, and DNA damage. Large amounts of these biomolecules cause cell death, but they can also induce normal cells to transform into malignant cells. 6 Furthermore, in CRPC with acquired ADT resistance, androgen deprivation causes an increase in ROS levels and the activation of AR signaling, suggesting that oxidative stress plays an important role in the growth mechanism of CRPC. 7 In other words, oxidative stress is involved in multiple stages of prostate carcinogenesis (Figure 2). Given this role of oxidative stress in prostate carcinogenesis, targeting this pathway through chemoprevention and therapeutic interventions represents a promising strategy to reduce carcinogenesis rates and improve patient outcomes.
</snippet>

Title: Identification of the oxidation stress-related gene signatures and functional verification of MINK1 in prostate cancer cells
Snippet: Prostate cancer (PCa) ranks as the second most frequently diagnosed malignancy among men [1]. The incidence of PCa has persistently remained high [2], contributing to an escalating social burden [3]. PCa is a typically heterogeneous disease [4]. There are significant differences in clinical manife stations among patients, some of which are accompanied by metastatic invasive diseases, while others are inert diseases that progress slowly [5]. Immunotherapy has emerged as a promising treatment modality for various malignancies [6][7][8][9][10][11]. However, in the context of PCa, its application is still under investigation, and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) continues to be the primary treatment approach during metastatic stages [12][13][14]. The long-term oncological outcomes for PCa patients vary considerably [15], underscoring the urgent need for novel biomarkers to inform the development of potential therapeutic strategies. 

Oxidative stress results from the disruption of homeostasis due to the excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) [16][17][18]. ROS are predominantly generated through the electron transport chain in mitochondria, as well as in peroxisomes and the endoplasmic reticulum, where protein oxidation occurs [19]. Previous research indicates that oxidative stress is involved in the development of multiple cancers, including bladder cancer [20], ovarian cancer [21], gastric cancer [22], and PCa [23,24]. Chronic oxidative stress, which is associated with the progression of invasive and metastatic diseases, plays a critical role in meeting the heightened metabolic demands resulting from the rapid proliferation of cancer cells [19,25]. Concurrently, ROS and cellular oxidative stress are produced excessively when cells are subjected to physical environments, cancer chemotherapy and radiotherapy [26,27]. In PCa, the continuous evolution of androgen receptor signaling can dynamically regulate the NRF2 activity related to oxidative stress and ROS levels [28]. Androgen receptor-targeted therapy has been shown to induce oxidative stress in PCa [29].
</snippet>

Title: Oxidative stress in prostate cancer patients: A systematic review of case control studies
Snippet: Background Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common cancer in men in Western countries. In-vitro and in-vivo studies suggest that oxidative stress (OS) and antioxidants play a key role in the pathogenesis of chronic diseases including PCa, which is promoted by the production of reactive oxygen species and impaired antioxidant defense mechanisms. This study evaluates the association between OS and men with PCa. Methods A literature search was carried out on Medline, PubMed, and ScienceDirect databases, as well as manual searches from inception up to August 2015 using the keywords “Oxidative stress” or “Reactive oxygen species” or “Lipid peroxidation” AND “Prostate cancer.” All studies including data on the measurement of OS biomarkers in PCa were included. Results Twenty-three case control studies were retrieved with sample sizes ranging from 15 to 3,613 (6,439 participants in total). Markers of OS were significantly higher in patients with PCa compared with control groups in 21 studies. Two self-controlled case studies comparing OS between PCa cells and non-PCa cells in tissue biopsies found OS to be statistically higher in PCa cancer cells. Results on markers of antioxidant capacity (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione, glutathione reductase, glutathione peroxidase, uric acid, lutein, lycopene, beta carotein, vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin E, and total antioxidants) were not completely consistent in their association with PCa. Conclusions Upregulated OS profiles and impairment of antioxidant defense systems may play a role in men with PCa. To confirm these findings, robust clinical trials utilizing a personalized approach which monitors both OS and antioxidant markers during therapy are warranted.
</snippet>

Title: Nitro aspirin (NCX4040) induces apoptosis in PC3 metastatic prostate cancer cells via hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-mediated oxidative stress
Snippet: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common second leading cause of cancer related deaths and the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men. 1 in 9 men will encounter PCa in their life time [1]. Non metastatic PCa has a five year survival rate of >99%, while patients with metastatic disease have only 28% five year survival rate [1]. Advanced PCa has high metastatic capabilities, originally arising as an androgen-dependent cancer. The disease progress to advanced stage as malignant cells transition into androgen independent, highly metastatic cells, which become resistant to hormonal therapy known as castration resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) [2][3][4]. Prostate cancer can be treated by surgery, radiation, androgen deprivation and chemotherapy depending on the status of cancer. Unfortunately standard therapies are unsuccessful in treating prostate cancer due to severe side effects, inflammation and chemo resistance. Therefore, it is important to identify the novel therapeutic agents for treating prostate cancer without inflammation.

Free radicals play an important role in living tissues to maintain cellular homeostasis of an organism. Imbalance in free radical levels leads to various pathological conditions [5]. The action of free radicals nullify by antioxidants/antioxidant enzymes present in the human body [6]. Antioxidant system includes catalase, glutathione (GSH), thioredoxins and vitamins. Lower levels or inactivation of antioxidants/enzymes in turn elevate the free radicals and results in the tumor formation by DNA damage, protein degradation and lipid peroxidation. Free radicals are unstable and highly reactive oxygen species. Free form of oxygen is required for all the aerobic organisms to maintain physiological functions and maintains healthy state. However, formation of free radicals responsible for tissue damage leads to disease state. Free radicals are composed of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) includes hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), hydroxyl (OH), and superoxide anion (O2 − ), nitric oxide (NO), peroxy nitrile (ONOO-) groups [7]. Most of the chemotherapeutic drugs show anticancer mechanism by inducing free radical generation

Title: Immunogenic Effect of Hyperthermia on Enhancing Radiotherapeutic Efficacy
Snippet: As the general regulator of hyperthermic stimulation, Hsps were upregulated and acted as signaling molecules and transcription factors upon heat shock. We found that some studies describing the role of Hsps in hyperthermia-induced radiosensitization suggested Hsps as the mediator of molecular events. Hyperthermia-induced Hsp72 expression increased the radio-and chemo-sensitivity of prostate cancer cells through the suppression of survival, MAPK, and NK-κB pathways [171]. This effect of combination therapy was also validated in an in vivo mouse prostate cancer model [172]. Hyperthermia also increased extracellular Hsps during tumor necrosis, which induced immunity against tumor cells [173]. However, some studies reported the roles of Hsp70 in radioresistance and Hsp72 in etoposide-induced apoptosis resistance [174,175]. This discrepancy suggested that hyperthermia-induced radiosensitization was partially dependent on Hsp expression. Taken together, these studies insisted that the underlying molecular mechanisms that mediate hyperthermia-induced radiosensitization are still elusive. Further molecular studies will be a key to the therapeutic optimization of hyperthermia as a radiosensitizing strategy.

At the molecular level, death occurs due to protein denaturation, DNA damage, and activation of various apoptotic pathways [123][124][125]. At the cellular level, heating also increases the release of heat shock proteins into the extracellular environment and increases the functional activity of innate immunity cells: NK killers (through NKG2D activation), macrophages, and dendritic cells [126][127][128]. Dendritic cells (DCs), in turn, take up heat shock protein/tumor antigen complexes, present tumor antigen to T cells and DC migration to lymph nodes, where T cells are activated in an MHC-dependent manner and delivered to tumor cells, passing through venules with high endothelium. Ultimately, activated CD8 + T cells attack and cause tumor cell death. 

Several authors showed the potency of nanothermotherapy for various in vivo tumor models: liver cancer [129], prostate cancer [130][131][132][133], brain or central nervous system cancers [134][135][136], and melanoma [122,137]. Magnetic hyperthermia is often used in combination with radiation therapy for tumor radiosensitization. This is due to the fact that hyperthermia increases perfusion and oxygenation of hypoxic tumor cells that are resistant to ionizing radiation. In addition, hyperthermia acts mainly at acidic pH and in the radioresistant S-phase of the cell cycle. This means that radiation therapy and hyperthermia complement each other; as a result of radiation therapy, formed free radicals damage the DNA of tumor cells, while hyperthermia inhibits its repair [138,139]. Despite a growing body of basic research and encouraging results both in vitro and in vivo, there are the technical difficulties of developing magnetic field applicators. Difficulty of maintaining frequencies and field characteristics suitable for clinical use, while adhering to the safety rules, is the main obstacle that holds the development of this method to clinical application [140].

Title: Thermal ablation in non-small cell lung cancer: a review of treatment modalities and the evidence for combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors
Snippet: Recent pre-clinical work and some clinical studies have suggested that percutaneous thermal ablative therapies may alter the immune-profile of patients with cancer by activating various steps in the cancer immunity cycle. This would imply that thermal ablation has the potential to improve the efficacy of immunotherapy (51,52). We will explore further the current evidence that supports this for RFA, cryoablation and MWA. 

Though evidence is limited in NSCLC, immunogenic changes with thermal ablation have been assessed in several malignancies, especially liver cancer, breast cancer, renal cell cancer and prostate cancer. Early studies in both cryoablation and RFA demonstrated tumour regression of untreated metastatic lesions (abscopal effect) with associated upregulation of immune cells in peripheral blood (53)(54)(55)(56)(57)(58)(59). 

Tumour necrosis occurs due to thermal ablation and results in neoantigen release from the tumour. RFA has been shown to increase carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels in liver metastasis of colorectal cancer and similar changes in serum prostate specific antigen (PSA) in prostate cancer has been seen with cryoablation (60,61). Along with an increase in neoantigen release, an upregulation of danger signals is seen and together this assists in modulating the first step of the cancer immunity cycle. Danger signals are endogenous molecules that are released by damaged cells and have various effects on cancer immunity. Heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) is a danger signal that has been found to be elevated post cryoablation and RFA in melanoma (62). Heat-shock proteins assists in antigen presenting, by both chaperoning antigen to dendritic cells and by upregulating MHC class 1 expression (63,64). This induction of neoantigen expression and danger signal release leads to increased neoantigen presentation as evidenced by the increased numbers of dendritic cells and enhanced dendritic cell maturation that has been observed with both cryoablation and RFA in several cancers including NSCLC (65,66).
</snippet>

Snippet: Hyperthermia is widely used to enhance the efficiency of chemotherapy or radiation in patients with inoperable cancer [31]. It has been given much attention for the cellular response to heat stress with respect to the immune system in cancer. The anti-tumor immune response can be markedly enhanced by treatment with hyperthermia particularly in the fever range [32]. Immunological effects of mild hyperthermia are twofold. One is the effect on dendritic and other immune cells [33]. The other is the effect is on tumor cells. Protein or peptides derived from cancer which are chaperoned by heat-shock protein (HSP) are possible sources of antigens, transferred to antigen presenting cells for priming CD8 + T cell responses [34]. Human tumor-derived HSP70 peptide complexes (HSP70-PC) have the immunogenic potential to instruct DCs and cross-present endogenously expressed, nonmutated, tumor antigenic peptides. The cross-presentation of a shared human tumor Ag together with its exquisite efficacy is an important new aspect for HSP70-based immunotherapy in clinical anticancer vaccination strategies, and suggest a potential extension of HSP70-based vaccination protocols from a patient-individual treatment modality to its use in an allogeneic setting [35]. The other studies support various clinical use of hyperthermia as part of an immunotherapeutic strategy in treating cancer [32,36]. 

The mechanisms by which a tumor cell can escape CTL is critical for the design and modification of effective vaccine strategies against cancer. These mechanisms fall into four broad categories: (i) inadequate antigen presentation by tumor cells resulting in their poor sensitivity to lysis by CTL; (ii) inhibitory signals provided by the tumor microenvironment; (iii) inability of TAA-specific CTL to localize at a tumor site; and (iv) inability of the tumor microenvironment to sustain T cell function in vivo [37]. Therefore, adequate antigen expression by tumor cells is of crucial importance. Many research papers show the possible augmentation of MHC class I antigen presentation via heat shock protein expression by hyperthermia.

Introduction and clinical context of deep microwave hyperthermia in prostate cancer
Deep microwave hyperthermia (DH) delivers localized, high-temperature heat (typically 40–47°C, often quantified as CEM43 in the 25–200 min range) to the prostate using microwave antennas or capacitive couplers, aiming to raise tumor temperatures while sparing normal tissue as much as possible. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heating of tumor cells in the 40–47 °C range with cumulative equivalent minutes at 43 °C (CEM43) of 25–200 min has been associated with radiosensitizing effects</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Microwave and radiofrequency hyperthermia generate heat via electromagnetic fields that drive water molecule rotation and frictional heating</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Radiofrequency capacitive hyperthermia is specifically recommended for prostate cancer due to cancer-versus-normal tissue autofocusing, where cancer’s physical properties cause preferential heating</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-2">In prostate modeling at 2.45 GHz, perfusion strongly modulates temperature distributions and necrosis, underscoring the need for accurate bioheat modeling to achieve deep tissue targets</cite>.

Core radiobiological mechanisms of thermoradiation synergy
1) DNA damage amplification and repair inhibition
<cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heat enhances radiosensitization by increasing DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and inhibiting DNA repair mechanisms, thereby intensifying radiation-induced toxicity</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">At 42–45 °C, hyperthermia is described as a potent radiosensitizer that can cause irreversible damage due to protein degradation and the lack of DSB repair in cells</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">In early combined modality experiments, 43 °C for 1 hour with single doses of 5–10 Gy produced higher cytotoxicity than radiation alone, and 10 Gy combined with 44 °C microwave heat significantly enhanced cell death in breast cancer models</cite>. Mechanistically, heat can directly damage DNA and also increase the formation of DSBs during or after irradiation, while concurrently suppressing key repair pathways such as non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR), thereby increasing the likelihood of lethal chromosomal aberrations. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Application of hyperthermia was reported to increase tumor radiosensitivity by enhancing DNA damage and inhibition of DNA repair mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">The additive effect of hyperthermia plus radiation can be quantified by the thermal enhancement factor (TEF), defined as the ratio of the response after radiation with heat to the response after radiation alone at the same dose</cite>.

2) Oxygenation and hypoxia modulation
<cite id="28e53f6b-0">Hyperthermia reduces hypoxia, thereby sensitizing radiation-resistant hypoxic tumor cells</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">The addition of heat to radiation inhibits DSB repair and intensifies radiation toxicity, with the radiosensitizing effect linked to improved oxygenation in hypoxic fractions</cite>. In prostate cancer, where hypoxia is common and linked to poor outcomes, microwave HT can preferentially raise tumor pO2 by heating and vascular effects, improving the effectiveness of fractionated RT that relies on oxygen-dependent repair pathways. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">High-energy photon RT (6–18 MV) is used for deeper prostate penetration, and combining heat with radiation is motivated by the need to overcome hypoxia in deep-seated tumors</cite>.

3) Cell-cycle, apoptosis, and heat shock protein (HSP) signaling
<cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heating can trigger apoptosis through inhibition of heat shock proteins and direct DNA damage</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Hyperthermia-induced upregulation of Hsp72 increases radio- and chemo-sensitivity of prostate cancer cells by suppressing survival, MAPK, and NF-κB pathways, and this radiosensitization has been validated in an in vivo mouse prostate cancer model</cite>. HSPs act as signaling and transcriptional mediators under heat stress; their induction can suppress pro-survival signaling that otherwise counteracts radiation-induced damage, thereby allowing more efficient execution of apoptotic programs following irradiation. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Concurrently, heat can increase extracellular HSPs during tumor necrosis, which induces immunity against tumor cells, but some studies report roles for Hsp70 and Hsp72 in radioresistance or apoptosis resistance, indicating that the net effect depends on expression levels and isoform-specific functions</cite>.

Non-thermal microwave electrophysiology and oxidative stress mechanisms
Beyond thermal dosimetry, microwave fields can induce non-thermal biological effects that potentiate radiation responses. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Microwave and radiofrequency heating rely on electromagnetic interactions with tissue water; precise dosimetry is challenging and reproducibility can be limited, but mechanistically heat production drives downstream cellular effects</cite>. <cite id="eb2fc70f-0">Prostate cancer cells exhibit elevated baseline oxidative stress and express ROS sources such as NOX enzymes and mitochondrial metabolism; tumor antioxidant capacity is often impaired, with increased lipid, protein, and nucleic acid oxidation correlating with aggressiveness</cite>. <cite id="eb2fc70f-1">Oxidative stress promotes DNA adducts, lipid peroxidation, protein carbonylation, mitochondrial abnormalities, and aberrant apoptosis, linking ROS accumulation to prostate carcinogenesis</cite>. Microwave-induced heating can further elevate mitochondrial ROS and perturb membrane/calcium homeostasis, augmenting radiation-induced oxidative DNA damage and impairing DNA repair enzymes and replication machinery during or after irradiation. <cite id="eb2fc70f-2">ROS and oxidative stress are excessively produced when cells are subjected to physical environments, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, and androgen receptor signaling dynamically regulates NRF2-mediated oxidative stress responses in PCa</cite>. <cite id="eb2fc70f-3">Systematic reviews in prostate cancer report significantly higher oxidative stress markers and impaired antioxidant defenses compared to controls, supporting a role for ROS-centric mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Microwave/radiofrequency hyperthermia has been shown to enhance radiosensitization via inhibition of DNA repair mechanisms and induction of apoptosis, consistent with oxidative and electrophysiologic perturbations that increase radiosensitivity</cite>.

Immune modulation: danger signals, antigen release, and dendritic-cell activation
Heat and thermal injury trigger immunogenic responses that can synergize with radiation. <cite id="bd38702b-1">Heat shock proteins act as chaperones that stimulate dendritic cell maturation and present tumor antigens, priming antigen-specific T cells; local tumor necrosis releases danger signals and neoantigens that are taken up by professional antigen-presenting cells, culminating in antitumor adaptive immunity</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Prostate cancer models demonstrate that hyperthermia-induced Hsp72 increases sensitivity to radio- and chemotherapy via suppression of survival signaling, and extracellular HSPs released during necrosis promote immunity against tumor cells</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-3">Thermal ablation in cancers including prostate increases PSA and induces upregulation of danger signals such as HSP70, with increased dendritic cell numbers and maturation, supporting enhanced antigen cross-presentation and T-cell priming</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-2">Heating increases extracellular HSP release and activates innate immune effector cells (NK cells via NKG2D, macrophages, and dendritic cells), enabling DC uptake of HSP/tumor antigen complexes, migration to lymph nodes, T-cell activation, and delivery of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells to tumors</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-4">Mild hyperthermia enhances anti-tumor immune responses by promoting HSP-mediated antigen cross-presentation and augmenting MHC class I antigen presentation, thereby improving CTL responses</cite>. Importantly, radiation can further amplify these immune effects, potentially enhancing immunogenic cell death and immune memory, while heat improves the quality and quantity of tumor antigens and danger cues presented to the immune system.

Tumor microenvironment: perfusion, necrosis/edema, and radiosensitization interplay
The depth and heterogeneity of prostate tumors impose constraints on heating and repair dynamics. <cite id="28e53f6b-2">Microwave (2.45 GHz) fields applied as internal sources show that blood perfusion critically shapes temperature distributions and the evolution of thermal damage, with higher perfusion increasing heat loss and altering necrotic percentages</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Early combined heat and radiation experiments showed enhanced cytotoxicity at clinically relevant temperatures (43 °C for 1 h) even when delivered during or around irradiation, suggesting that perfusion-mediated heat dissipation can be managed to achieve synergistic effects</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-2">Hyperthermia increases perfusion and oxygenation of hypoxic tumor cells, and acts in acidic pH and the radioresistant S-phase, complementing radiation whose free-radical DNA damage is potentiated by heat-inhibited repair</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heating can also reduce hypoxia and induce apoptosis via HSP inhibition, thereby increasing the fraction of cells irreversibly damaged by ionizing radiation</cite>. Clinically, heat-driven edema and transient perfusion changes must be managed around RT to avoid dose interruptions; modeling-guided planning and temperature monitoring can mitigate these effects and preserve synergy.

Scheduling, dose, and prostate-specific translational evidence
Prostate trials of capacitive RF/microwave HT typically deliver heat pre- or post-RT to enhance DSB effects or sensitize sublethal repair. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Prostate RF capacitive HT at 13.56 MHz induces preferential tissue heating via dielectric coupling, and combined modality studies show that heat before or after irradiation can enhance radiation damage; the TEF quantifies this synergy, with studies in prostate cancer cells exploring pre- and post-treatment schedules</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">In combined water-bath hyperthermia with RT, cytotoxicity peaked after 43 °C for 1 hour followed by 5–10 Gy, and microwave heat at 44 °C for 1 hour with 10 Gy significantly increased cell death hours later, supporting a time-dependent radiosensitization mechanism</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">High-dose photon RT is commonly used in prostate cancer; pairing heat with radiation leverages heat’s inhibition of DSB repair and its capacity to increase protein degradation, aligning with clinical efforts to escalate doses while controlling toxicity</cite>.

Mechanistic biomarkers and clinical predictors
Several candidate biomarkers may predict responsiveness to thermoradiation in prostate cancer. <cite id="eb2fc70f-0">NRF2 and related antioxidant pathways regulate ROS and metabolic shifts in PCa; oxidative stress levels and antioxidant capacity vary with disease aggressiveness, suggesting that tumors with higher basal ROS and impaired antioxidant defenses may be more radiosensitizable to heat</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">HSP72 induction and suppression of survival/MAPK/NF-κB pathways enhance radio-sensitivity in prostate models, whereas HSP70 or HSP72-mediated resistance has been reported in some contexts, implying isoform- and expression-dependent effects</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heating-induced inhibition of heat shock proteins and direct DNA damage promotes apoptosis, but the precise balance depends on the tumor’s thermoresistance and repair capacity</cite>. Clinically, reproducibility and dosimetry constraints remain: <cite id="28e53f6b-0">electromagnetic-wave HT methods can lack precision in target definition and allow only limited quantification of thermal dose without MR temperature mapping, highlighting the need for robust thermometry and quality assurance</cite>.

Putting it together: how deep microwave hyperthermia sensitizes prostate tumors to radiation
- Heat increases DSB formation and directly damages DNA, while suppressing non-homologous end joining and homologous recombination, leading to higher rates of misrepair or no-repair after irradiation. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Enhancing DNA damage and inhibiting DNA repair mechanisms under hyperthermia intensifies radiation-induced toxicity</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">At 42–45 °C, inhibition of DSB repair amplifies radiation damage</cite>.
- Microwave HT preferentially elevates tumor oxygenation and targets hypoxic subvolumes, improving oxygen-dependent repair inhibition and the efficacy of photon RT in deep-seated prostate tissue. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Heat reduces hypoxia and increases radiosensitivity</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Radiation-induced DSBs are potentiated by heat that inhibits repair, with hypoxia as a key mediator</cite>.
- Electrophysiologic and oxidative effects from microwave heating (membrane/calcium perturbations, mitochondrial ROS) degrade DNA repair capacity and promote apoptosis, especially when aligned with irradiation timing. <cite id="eb2fc70f-0">ROS sources and impaired antioxidant defenses are intrinsic to aggressive PCa</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">Microwave/radiofrequency heating enhances radiosensitization via repair inhibition and apoptosis induction</cite>.
- Heat-induced HSPs and DAMPs create a pro-immune microenvironment: extracellular HSPs, neoantigen release, and dendritic-cell maturation enhance CTL responses, which can amplify radiation-induced immunogenic cell death and drive systemic antitumor immunity. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Hsp72-mediated suppression of survival signaling increases radiosensitivity in prostate models and extracellular HSPs promote immunity</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-1">HSPs chaperone antigens to DCs and drive T-cell priming</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-3">Prostate ablation increases PSA and induces HSP70 upregulation with increased dendritic cell maturation</cite>.
- Delivery physics and tumor physics shape synergy: deep microwave applicators (endorectal/corporal or interstitial antennas) must overcome perfusion cooling to reach 40–43 °C targets in the prostate, and TEF-based scheduling (pre- vs post-RT) can be optimized to maximize DSB fixation and minimize repair. <cite id="28e53f6b-2">Perfusion strongly modulates deep-tissue heating and necrosis</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">TEF quantifies the additive effect of heat and radiation, with prostate-specific scheduling studies guiding pre/post-irradiation strategies</cite>.

Clinical integration and open questions
<cite id="28e53f6b-0">Early combined hyperthermia–radiation studies in prostate and other models demonstrate significant enhancement of cytotoxicity at clinically achievable temperatures (43–44 °C for 1 h) and doses (5–10 to 10 Gy)</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Capacitive RF HT is recommended for prostate cancer due to autofocusing and preferential tumor heating, and the TEF framework is used to estimate and schedule synergistic gains</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">However, technical challenges remain in targeting precision and thermal dosimetry for electromagnetic-wave HT, with better thermometry (e.g., MR temperature mapping) enabling more reproducible, quantifiable dose delivery</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">HSP-mediated effects can be both beneficial and maladaptive depending on isoform and expression levels, indicating a need for biomarker-driven patient selection</cite>. <cite id="eb2fc70f-0">Given the central role of oxidative stress in PCa progression and treatment resistance, combining microwave HT with strategies that further elevate ROS while normalizing antioxidant capacity may maximize radiosensitization</cite>.

Summary
Deep microwave hyperthermia sensitizes prostate tumors to radiation through a coordinated set of thermal and non-thermal mechanisms: heat amplifies radiation-induced DNA damage while inhibiting repair, improves oxygenation in hypoxic prostate regions, triggers apoptosis via HSP modulation, and induces non-thermal electrophysiologic and oxidative perturbations that degrade repair capacity. <cite id="28e53f6b-0">These effects occur at clinically relevant temperatures (40–47 °C; CEM43 25–200 min) and have been demonstrated to increase cytotoxicity over RT alone in vitro and in vivo</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-4">Prostate-focused RF/microwave HT leverages these pathways, with TEF-based scheduling and perfusion-aware delivery to enhance radiosensitization</cite>. <cite id="bd38702b-0">Immune mechanisms mediated by HSPs and DAMPs further potentiate antitumor immunity, creating a dual cytotoxic and immunologic synergy with radiation</cite>. <cite id="28e53f6b-2">Ultimately, modeling and clinical engineering must align deep tissue perfusion with thermal dose to ensure that these mechanistic advantages translate into reproducible, safe, and effective gains in prostate radiotherapy outcomes</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Focused ultrasound radiosensitizes human cancer cells by enhancement of DNA damage
Snippet: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in males in Europe and metastatic prostate cancer can lead to incapacitating pain and fractures. As examples of highly aggressive cancer entities, head and neck tumors, glioblastoma, and metastatic prostate cancer subtypes require novel and more effective treatment regimens, and were thereby chosen in our study. 

To enhance the treatment outcome, reduce radiation dose, and simultaneously avoid radiation-induced adverse effects, growing interest lies on the radiosensitization of the tumor cells. Heating of tumor cells up to high temperatures (40-47 °C) in a thermal dose cumulative equivalent minutes at 43 °C (CEM43) range of 25-200 min showed beneficial radiosensitizing effects [12,18]. The underlying mechanism of RT is the induction of DNA double-strand breaks leading to cell death [19]. Application of HT was reported to increase the tumor radiosensitivity by enhancing DNA damage, inhibition of DNA repair mechanism, and reduction of hypoxia [20,21]. Different mechanisms like induction of apoptosis mediated by an inhibition of heat shock proteins [22,23] or directly by damage of DNA [24] are also described as leading to radiosensitization effects. 

Currently, HT is mostly delivered by microwave, radiofrequency, or FUS in clinic. Microwave and radiofrequency generate heating by electromagnetic waves causing rotation of water molecules in cells, inducing frictional heating [25]. In early 1989, the effect of combined water bath HT and RT was published: higher cytotoxicity was observed 24 h after exposure to 43 °C for 1 h and single-dose radiation at 5-10 Gy compared to RT alone [26]. Snippet: The development of hyperthermia-based therapy for prostate cancer requires precise modeling of the thermal behavior of biological tissues. In order to simulate healthy tissue, this study creates a computational model of a prostate tumor that is shaped like a spherical area encircled by another concentric sphere. The investigation focuses on the effects of blood perfusion rate fluctuations on the temperature distribution and subsequent thermal damage in the surrounding tissue and tumor. The heating source is modeled as a collection of electric dipoles at the center of the tumor that are subjected to a microwave (2.45 GHz) alternating electromagnetic field. The temporal evolution of temperature and tissue necros is under varying perfusion rates is described using the Arrhenius damage model and the Pennes bioheat transfer equation. Title: NRF2: A crucial regulator for mitochondrial metabolic shift and prostate cancer progression
Snippet: Increased oxidative stress is required for increased invasiveness in metastatic PCa (B. Kumar et al., 2008). Prostate cancer cells can produce ROS from NADPH oxidases (NOX), mitochondrial metabolism as well as endoplasmic reticulum stress (Khandrika et al., 2009;Costanzo-Garvey et al., 2022). The following studies support that oxidative stress increases as PCa progresses and that the increased oxidative stress support PCa aggressiveness. In one study, reduction of ROS by diphenyleneiodonium chloride blocked PCa cell proliferation by blocking ERK, p38 and AKT signaling and caused cyclin B-dependent G2M cell cycle arrest (B. Kumar et al., 2008). In another study, increased oxidation of macromolecules such as, lipids, proteins and nucleic acid were used to measure oxidative stress and showed increased oxidation correlates with aggressiveness of PCa (Zha et al., 2005;Kalinina et al., 2022). Polymorphisms in the genes related to oxidative stress and antioxidant response were also investigated in the PCa patient's blood and polymorphisms that change the function of NQO1 and SOD2 are positively associated with prostate carcinogenesis (Gong Z et al., 2021;Z. Zhang et al., 2019). SOD, GSH, and CAT activity were significantly lower and serum levels of malondialdehyde were significantly higher in prostate cancer patients as compared to healthy controls (Ahmed Amar et al., 2019). In another study, SOD activity was found to be higher in PCa patients as compared to healthy population whereas levels of thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS), protein carbonylation, were significantly higher in PCa patients (Battisti et al., 2011). This indicates that SOD protein was enhanced to try to combat the high levels of oxidative stress in tumors, but the antioxidant scavenging system was still overwhelmed.

Title: Exploring experimental models of prostate cancer in chemoprevention: Oxidative stress as a key pathway to translational research
Snippet: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most common cancer in men globally, as well as a leading cause of cancer-related death. 1 PCa is positive for androgen receptor (AR) expression, and it exhibits androgendependent growth. 2 Thus, this malignancy significantly responds to androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT). However, castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), which has acquired castration-resistant growth, is metastatic and carries a poor prognosis. The process by which normal prostate cells become malignant involves a combination of various factors, including congenital factors determined by race, region, and genetics, 3,4 environmental factors such as dietary and other lifestyle habits; and acquired factors such as genetic changes. 

In particular, aging and diet and lifestyle habits can lead to changes in the endocrine environment of the prostate gland and chronic inflammation, which are associated with PCa development. An important mechanism of PCa development and progression is 'oxidative stress,' which arises from a redox imbalance between the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and activity of antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase (GPX, Figure 1). 5 Excessive ROS accumulation promotes the development of DNA adducts, lipid peroxidation, and protein carbonylation through the oxidation of nucleic acids and lipids, resulting in mitochondrial abnormalities, abnormal apoptosis, and DNA damage. Large amounts of these biomolecules cause cell death, but they can also induce normal cells to transform into malignant cells. 6 Furthermore, in CRPC with acquired ADT resistance, androgen deprivation causes an increase in ROS levels and the activation of AR signaling, suggesting that oxidative stress plays an important role in the growth mechanism of CRPC. 7 In other words, oxidative stress is involved in multiple stages of prostate carcinogenesis (Figure 2). Given this role of oxidative stress in prostate carcinogenesis, targeting this pathway through chemoprevention and therapeutic interventions represents a promising strategy to reduce carcinogenesis rates and improve patient outcomes.

Title: Identification of the oxidation stress-related gene signatures and functional verification of MINK1 in prostate cancer cells
Snippet: Prostate cancer (PCa) ranks as the second most frequently diagnosed malignancy among men [1]. The incidence of PCa has persistently remained high [2], contributing to an escalating social burden [3]. PCa is a typically heterogeneous disease [4]. There are significant differences in clinical manife stations among patients, some of which are accompanied by metastatic invasive diseases, while others are inert diseases that progress slowly [5]. Immunotherapy has emerged as a promising treatment modality for various malignancies [6][7][8][9][10][11]. However, in the context of PCa, its application is still under investigation, and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) continues to be the primary treatment approach during metastatic stages [12][13][14]. The long-term oncological outcomes for PCa patients vary considerably [15], underscoring the urgent need for novel biomarkers to inform the development of potential therapeutic strategies. 

Oxidative stress results from the disruption of homeostasis due to the excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) [16][17][18]. ROS are predominantly generated through the electron transport chain in mitochondria, as well as in peroxisomes and the endoplasmic reticulum, where protein oxidation occurs [19]. Previous research indicates that oxidative stress is involved in the development of multiple cancers, including bladder cancer [20], ovarian cancer [21], gastric cancer [22], and PCa [23,24]. Chronic oxidative stress, which is associated with the progression of invasive and metastatic diseases, plays a critical role in meeting the heightened metabolic demands resulting from the rapid proliferation of cancer cells [19,25]. Concurrently, ROS and cellular oxidative stress are produced excessively when cells are subjected to physical environments, cancer chemotherapy and radiotherapy [26,27]. In PCa, the continuous evolution of androgen receptor signaling can dynamically regulate the NRF2 activity related to oxidative stress and ROS levels [28]. Androgen receptor-targeted therapy has been shown to induce oxidative stress in PCa [29].

Title: Oxidative stress in prostate cancer patients: A systematic review of case control studies
Snippet: Background Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common cancer in men in Western countries. In-vitro and in-vivo studies suggest that oxidative stress (OS) and antioxidants play a key role in the pathogenesis of chronic diseases including PCa, which is promoted by the production of reactive oxygen species and impaired antioxidant defense mechanisms. This study evaluates the association between OS and men with PCa. Methods A literature search was carried out on Medline, PubMed, and ScienceDirect databases, as well as manual searches from inception up to August 2015 using the keywords “Oxidative stress” or “Reactive oxygen species” or “Lipid peroxidation” AND “Prostate cancer.” All studies including data on the measurement of OS biomarkers in PCa were included. Results Twenty-three case control studies were retrieved with sample sizes ranging from 15 to 3,613 (6,439 participants in total). Markers of OS were significantly higher in patients with PCa compared with control groups in 21 studies. Two self-controlled case studies comparing OS between PCa cells and non-PCa cells in tissue biopsies found OS to be statistically higher in PCa cancer cells. Results on markers of antioxidant capacity (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione, glutathione reductase, glutathione peroxidase, uric acid, lutein, lycopene, beta carotein, vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin E, and total antioxidants) were not completely consistent in their association with PCa. Conclusions Upregulated OS profiles and impairment of antioxidant defense systems may play a role in men with PCa. To confirm these findings, robust clinical trials utilizing a personalized approach which monitors both OS and antioxidant markers during therapy are warranted.

Title: Nitro aspirin (NCX4040) induces apoptosis in PC3 metastatic prostate cancer cells via hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-mediated oxidative stress
Snippet: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common second leading cause of cancer related deaths and the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men. 1 in 9 men will encounter PCa in their life time [1]. Non metastatic PCa has a five year survival rate of >99%, while patients with metastatic disease have only 28% five year survival rate [1]. Advanced PCa has high metastatic capabilities, originally arising as an androgen-dependent cancer. The disease progress to advanced stage as malignant cells transition into androgen independent, highly metastatic cells, which become resistant to hormonal therapy known as castration resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) [2][3][4]. Prostate cancer can be treated by surgery, radiation, androgen deprivation and chemotherapy depending on the status of cancer. Unfortunately standard therapies are unsuccessful in treating prostate cancer due to severe side effects, inflammation and chemo resistance. Therefore, it is important to identify the novel therapeutic agents for treating prostate cancer without inflammation.

Free radicals play an important role in living tissues to maintain cellular homeostasis of an organism. Imbalance in free radical levels leads to various pathological conditions [5]. The action of free radicals nullify by antioxidants/antioxidant enzymes present in the human body [6]. Antioxidant system includes catalase, glutathione (GSH), thioredoxins and vitamins. Lower levels or inactivation of antioxidants/enzymes in turn elevate the free radicals and results in the tumor formation by DNA damage, protein degradation and lipid peroxidation. Free radicals are unstable and highly reactive oxygen species. Free form of oxygen is required for all the aerobic organisms to maintain physiological functions and maintains healthy state. However, formation of free radicals responsible for tissue damage leads to disease state. Free radicals are composed of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) includes hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), hydroxyl (OH), and superoxide anion (O2 − ), nitric oxide (NO), peroxy nitrile (ONOO-) groups [7]. Most of the chemotherapeutic drugs show anticancer mechanism by inducing free radical generation

Advanced PCa has high metastatic capabilities, originally arising as an androgen-dependent cancer. The disease progress to advanced stage as malignant cells transition into androgen independent, highly metastatic cells, which become resistant to hormonal therapy known as castration resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) [2][3][4]. Prostate cancer can be treated by surgery, radiation, androgen deprivation and chemotherapy depending on the status of cancer. Unfortunately standard therapies are unsuccessful in treating prostate cancer due to severe side effects, inflammation and chemo resistance. Therefore, it is important to identify the novel therapeutic agents for treating prostate cancer without inflammation.

Free radicals play an important role in living tissues to maintain cellular homeostasis of an organism. Imbalance in free radical levels leads to various pathological conditions [5]. The action of free radicals nullify by antioxidants/antioxidant enzymes present in the human body [6]. Antioxidant system includes catalase, glutathione (GSH), thioredoxins and vitamins. Lower levels or inactivation of antioxidants/enzymes in turn elevate the free radicals and results in the tumor formation by DNA damage, protein degradation and lipid peroxidation. Free radicals are unstable and highly reactive oxygen species. Free form of oxygen is required for all the aerobic organisms to maintain physiological functions and maintains healthy state. However, formation of free radicals responsible for tissue damage leads to disease state. Free radicals are composed of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) includes hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), hydroxyl (OH), and superoxide anion (O2 − ), nitric oxide (NO), peroxy nitrile (ONOO-) groups [7]. Most of the chemotherapeutic drugs show anticancer mechanism by inducing free radical generation

documents.snippet: Increased oxidative stress is required for increased invasiveness in metastatic PCa (B. Kumar et al., 2008). Prostate cancer cells can produce ROS from NADPH oxidases (NOX), mitochondrial metabolism as well as endoplasmic reticulum stress (Khandrika et al., 2009;Costanzo-Garvey et al., 2022). The following studies support that oxidative stress increases as PCa progresses and that the increased oxidative stress support PCa aggressiveness. In one study, reduction of ROS by diphenyleneiodonium chloride blocked PCa cell proliferation by blocking ERK, p38 and AKT signaling and caused cyclin B-dependent G2M cell cycle arrest (B. Kumar et al., 2008). In another study, increased oxidation of macromolecules such as, lipids, proteins and nucleic acid were used to measure oxidative stress and showed increased oxidation correlates with aggressiveness of PCa (Zha et al., 2005;Kalinina et al., 2022). Polymorphisms in the genes related to oxidative stress and antioxidant response were also investigated in the PCa patient's blood and polymorphisms that change the function of NQO1 and SOD2 are positively associated with prostate carcinogenesis (Gong Z et al., 2021;Z. Zhang et al., 2019). SOD, GSH, and CAT activity were significantly lower and serum levels of malondialdehyde were significantly higher in prostate cancer patients as compared to healthy controls (Ahmed Amar et al., 2019). In another study, SOD activity was found to be higher in PCa patients as compared to healthy population whereas levels of thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS), protein carbonylation, were significantly higher in PCa patients (Battisti et al., 2011). This indicates that SOD protein was enhanced to try to combat the high levels of oxidative stress in tumors, but the antioxidant scavenging system was still overwhelmed.

documents.title: Exploring experimental models of prostate cancer in chemoprevention: Oxidative stress as a key pathway to translational research
documents.snippet:
Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most common cancer in men globally, as well as a leading cause of cancer-related death. 1 PCa is positive for androgen receptor (AR) expression, and it exhibits androgendependent growth. 2 Thus, this malignancy significantly responds to androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT). However, castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), which has acquired castration-resistant growth, is metastatic and carries a poor prognosis. The process by which normal prostate cells become malignant involves a combination of various factors, including congenital factors determined by race, region, and genetics, 3,4 environmental factors such as dietary and other lifestyle habits; and acquired factors such as genetic changes. 

In particular, aging and diet and lifestyle habits can lead to changes in the endocrine environment of the prostate gland and chronic inflammation, which are associated with PCa development. An important mechanism of PCa development and progression is 'oxidative stress,' which arises from a redox imbalance between the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and activity of antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase (GPX, Figure 1). 5 Excessive ROS accumulation promotes the development of DNA adducts, lipid peroxidation, and protein carbonylation through the oxidation of nucleic acids and lipids, resulting in mitochondrial abnormalities, abnormal apoptosis, and DNA damage. Large amounts of these biomolecules cause cell death, but they can also induce normal cells to transform into malignant cells. 6 Furthermore, in CRPC with acquired ADT resistance, androgen deprivation causes an increase in ROS levels and the activation of AR signaling, suggesting that oxidative stress plays an important role in the growth mechanism of CRPC. 7 In other words, oxidative stress is involved in multiple stages of prostate carcinogenesis (Figure 2). Given this role of oxidative stress in prostate carcinogenesis, targeting this pathway through chemoprevention and therapeutic interventions represents a promising strategy to reduce carcinogenesis rates and improve patient outcomes.
